column2: On the authority of Abū Mālik al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀṣim al-Ashʿarī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said: “Purification is half of faith. Al-ḥamdu lillāh fills the Balance,

and subḥān Allāh and al-ḥamdu lillāh fill—or: fills—what is between the heavens and the earth. Prayer is light, charity is proof, patience is radiance, and the Qurʾān is an argument for you or against you.
Every person goes out in the morning and sells himself, either freeing it or destroying it.” Reported by Muslim.
Al-ṭuhūr (“purification”): with ḍammah on the ṭāʾ; purifying oneself with water from ritual impurities.

Shaṭr al-īmān (“half of faith”): because the qualities of faith are of two kinds: one purifies and cleanses the heart, and the other purifies the outward; so in this respect they are two halves. There are other views on how purification is half of faith, and Allah knows best what His Messenger meant.
“Fills the Balance”: because of the greatness of its reward. The reason for this is that praising [Allah] is affirming all praise for Allah.

“Fill—or: fills—what is between the heavens and the earth”: if their reward were given bodily form, it would fill what is between the heaven and the earth, because they contain declaring Allah free [of imperfection] and praising Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The “or” is due to the narrator's doubt.
Al-ṣalāh (“prayer”): that which fulfils its conditions and what completes it,
nūr (“is light”): by it the believer's heart is illuminated in this world, its radiance may show on his face, and it will be a light for him in the darkness of the Day of Resurrection.
“Charity is proof”: an argument for its doer's belief in the recompense of the Day of Resurrection, because the hypocrite holds back from it, not believing that there is any reward in it.
Al-ṣabr (“patience”): the praiseworthy kind, which is patience in obeying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, patience in refraining from sins, and patience with painful decrees.
“And the Qurʾān is an argument for you”: it guides you to salvation if you act on it,
“or against you”: if you turn away from it, it points to your evil end.
Yaghdū (“goes out in the morning”): strives with himself,
“and sells himself”: to Allah by obeying Him,
“freeing it”: from punishment,
“or destroying it”: ruining it by selling it to the devil and to whims by following them.
The printed text reads قسين and تصفان, evidently for قسمين (“two kinds”) and نصفان (“two halves”).
The virtue of purification.
The virtue of glorifying and praising [Allah].
Affirmation of the Balance by which deeds will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection.
The great reward of prayer, charity and patience.
Whoever follows the Qurʾān, it leads him to Paradise; and whoever puts it behind his back and turns away from it is cast into the Fire.
Every person is striving either to destroy himself or to free himself. Whoever strives in obedience to Allah has sold himself to Allah
and freed himself from His punishment; and whoever strives in disobedience to Allah has sold himself for humiliation and destroyed himself with sins that bring the anger and punishment of Allah.
